subject: film
title: Taiwan New Cinema (c. 1982–1990s): local lives after martial-era studio habits
dek: Under martial law the Central Motion Picture Corporation had taught audiences healthy-realism and commercial genres. In the 1980s a younger generation, still often CMPC-backed, turned the camera onto Taipei streets, coming-of-age, and histories that had been hard to name — then learned to travel through festivals.

thumb.alt: Hou Hsiao-hsien in 1989, short hair, dark jacket, looking slightly off-camera.

hero.alt: Hou Hsiao-hsien standing outdoors in 1989 at the Venice Film Festival, holding the Golden Lion statuette.
hero.caption: Hou Hsiao-hsien with the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival, 1989, after A City of Sadness. The statue in his hands is the festival's top prize. The photograph is a festival portrait, not a frame from the film.
hero.credit: Gorup de Besanez / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

honesty: “Taiwan New Cinema” (台灣新電影) is a historians’ and critics’ name for a cluster of films and people from about 1982 into the early 1990s, not a union card and not a single manifesto that started the cameras. Many of the early features were still financed or released through the Central Motion Picture Corporation. Martial law ended on 15 July 1987; the films did not flip overnight with that date. The 1987 “Taiwan Cinema Manifesto” (also called the “Another Cinema” manifesto) was a public fight over policy, media, and criticism as much as a style sheet — and many writers treat it as a hinge toward the end of the first wave, not its birth certificate. French New Wave is a name that traveled; New Hollywood was the American industrial mode ending into blockbusters in the same calendar years. Neither is a template this lesson copies shot for shot. Film stills are usually still in copyright, so the pictures here are festival portraits, later memorials, and free exteriors, captioned as what they actually show. No AI people.

timeline.label: Studio habits
timeline.detail: CMPC’s healthy-realism line and commercial genres (including Qiong Yao melodramas) under martial law. Hong Kong and Hollywood imports take much of the box office. “National cinema” often means Mandarin, party-aligned, and exportable to overseas Chinese markets.

timeline.label: In Our Time
timeline.detail: CMPC omnibus In Our Time (光陰的故事): segments by Tao Te-chen, Edward Yang, Ko I-chen, and Chang Yi. Widely treated as the opening date for Taiwan New Cinema.

timeline.label: Early CMPC turns
timeline.detail: Growing Up (小畢的故事) and the omnibus The Sandwich Man (兒子的大玩偶). Hou Hsiao-hsien, Wan Jen, and others move from script and segment work into features that look and sound unlike healthy-realism.

timeline.label: Taipei films / manifesto / martial law
timeline.detail: Yang’s Taipei Story (1985) and The Terrorizers (1986). Hou’s Dust in the Wind (1986). The Taiwan Cinema Manifesto is drafted around late 1986 and published January 1987. Martial law is lifted 15 July 1987.

timeline.label: Venice
timeline.detail: Hou’s A City of Sadness wins the Golden Lion at Venice — the first Taiwanese film to take the prize. 2/28 reaches a wide screen.

timeline.label: Late first wave / Second New Wave edge
timeline.detail: Yang’s A Brighter Summer Day (1991). Hou’s The Puppetmaster (1993). Tsai Ming-liang’s early features begin to define a Second New Wave aftershock in the early 1990s.

fun_fact.title: A City of Sadness was the first Taiwanese Golden Lion
fun_fact.text: At the 46th Venice Film Festival in September 1989, Hou Hsiao-hsien’s A City of Sadness won the Golden Lion — Venice’s top prize. It was the first Taiwanese film to take that award. The film had already made a different kind of history at home: it was the first Taiwanese feature to put the February 28 Incident of 1947 openly on screen for a wide audience, two years after martial law ended. Festival travel and domestic argument arrived in the same season.

image.alt: Hou Hsiao-hsien holding the Golden Lion at Venice in 1989.
image.caption: Hou with the Golden Lion, Venice 1989. The prize is metal and concrete in the photograph; the film’s subject — 2/28 and the years around it — is what the prize was arguing for internationally.
image.credit: Gorup de Besanez / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

glossary.explain: Critics’ and historians’ name for a cluster of Taiwanese films and filmmakers from about 1982 into the early 1990s: location shooting, understated acting, coming-of-age and urban Taipei, and nativist-literature adaptations, often still linked to CMPC money at the start.

Central Motion Picture Corporation, the major state-linked studio under the Kuomintang. It produced healthy-realism and commercial genres for decades, then financed early New Cinema omnibuses and features such as In Our Time.

CMPC production line from the 1960s associated with studio head Kung Hung: films that looked “realistic” in texture while avoiding dark social exposure and promoting positive, humanitarian values. A studio habit, not a free press.

In Taiwan, the period of Kuomintang emergency rule lasting from 1949 until 15 July 1987. Film scripts, speech, and public history were constrained; New Cinema’s early years sit partly inside that frame and partly after it.

Common name for political repression under martial-law Taiwan: arrests, imprisonment, and executions of real or suspected dissidents. The term is wider than any single incident; 2/28 is an earlier hinge often linked to it in public memory.

The February 28 Incident of 1947: protests after a Tobacco Monopoly crackdown, then violent suppression by Nationalist forces newly administering Taiwan. Thousands were killed. A City of Sadness (1989) was the first Taiwanese feature to put it openly on a wide screen.

Taiwanese literary current of the 1970s emphasizing local language, class, and place against purely mainland-centered or high-Mandarin culture. New Cinema adapted several of these stories; The Sandwich Man draws on Huang Chun-ming.

A shot that runs without a cut for an unusually long time. In Taiwan New Cinema criticism, long takes are often read as a way to watch social time pass — waiting, walking, a family meal — instead of chopping action into Hollywood continuity beats.

The dominant classical editing style that matches eyelines, keeps geography clear, and moves the story beat by beat. New Cinema critics and filmmakers often worked against that tempo: longer shots, fewer explanatory cuts, more time left on the table.
Filming in real streets, houses, and landscapes rather than rebuilding everything on a soundstage. Taipei apartments, Jiufen hills, and ordinary rooms are part of how New Cinema looked “local.”
The top prize of the Venice Film Festival. A City of Sadness won it in 1989 — the first Taiwanese film to do so.
Major European film festival on the Lido. For Taiwan New Cinema it was a path out: festival prizes made films travel when the domestic market was thinning.

Public statement drafted around late 1986 and published in January 1987. Roughly fifty signatories asked for space for “another cinema” against unclear policy, entertainment-first media, and hostile criticism. Many historians treat it as a hinge near the end of the first wave.
1982 CMPC omnibus with segments by Tao Te-chen, Edward Yang, Ko I-chen, and Chang Yi. Conventional starting date for Taiwan New Cinema.
1983 CMPC-backed feature (Chen Kun-hou directing; Hou Hsiao-hsien among the writers). An early turn toward everyday coming-of-age rather than healthy-realism uplift.
1983 CMPC omnibus adapting Huang Chun-ming stories; segments by Hou Hsiao-hsien, Tseng Chuang-hsiang, and Wan Jen.
1989 Hou Hsiao-hsien feature about a Taiwanese family across the mid-1940s, including 2/28. Golden Lion at Venice 1989.
1985 Edward Yang feature. Hou Hsiao-hsien acts opposite Tsai Chin. A mournful account of a couple and a city caught between property, baseball nostalgia, and a changing Taipei.
1986 Edward Yang feature. Interlocking Taipei lives, photography, and chance; urban form as the subject, not only the backdrop.
1991 Edward Yang epic about four hours set in early-1960s Taipei, centered on youth, gangs, rock and roll, and a real murder case. Late first-wave monument.
1986 Hou feature: young people leave Jiufen for work in Taipei.
2000 Edward Yang family film, often a late summation rather than a New Cinema starter.
1993 Hou film about Li Tian-lu and glove-theatre life under Japanese rule. Long takes and staged testimony; Jury Prize at Cannes.
1994 Tsai Ming-liang feature about empty apartments and lonely orbits in Taipei. Golden Lion at Venice 1994. Second New Wave aftershock, not the 1982 opening.
1983 Edward Yang first feature. Sylvia Chang among the leads; friendship, marriage, and class in a modernizing Taiwan.
1987 Hou feature set in contemporary Taipei: night work, family strain, neon.
Taiwanese director, central New Cinema figure. From Sandwich Man and Dust in the Wind through A City of Sadness and later features. Also acted in Yang’s Taipei Story.
Taiwanese director. Segment in In Our Time; features including That Day on the Beach, Taipei Story, The Terrorizers, A Brighter Summer Day, and later Yi Yi.
Malaysian-born Taiwanese director. Emerges in the early 1990s as Second New Wave aftershock: even longer takes, empty rooms, Lee Kang-sheng as recurring presence.
Director associated with New Cinema-era CMPC and literary adaptations. Part of the wider field, not only the Hou-Yang duo.
Director; segment of The Sandwich Man (1983) and later features. One of the early omnibus names that made New Cinema look like a collective turn.
Writer, later director. CMPC script department; co-wrote key Hou films including Dust in the Wind and A City of Sadness.
Actor, producer, and later director. Appears in Yang’s That Day on the Beach and other 1980s work; a star-producer presence in the New Cinema years.
Writer; long-time Hou collaborator, including A City of Sadness and Daughter of the Nile.
Writer and CMPC figure who helped push early 1980s projects such as In Our Time when the domestic industry was losing audiences.
CMPC general manager in the period when the studio backed early New Cinema omnibuses.
CMPC president associated with launching the healthy-realism production line in the 1960s.
Cinematographer-director; directed Growing Up (1983).
Director; one of four In Our Time segment directors (1982).
Director; In Our Time segment; later New Cinema-era features.
Director; In Our Time segment director.
Director; segment of The Sandwich Man (1983).
Nativist writer. Stories adapted in The Sandwich Man omnibus.
Glove-theatre performer and actor. Subject and on-screen presence in Hou 1993 film 戲夢人生; also appears in other Hou films.
Hong Kong actor; plays the mute photographer Wen-ching in A City of Sadness.
Singer-actor; leads Taipei Story opposite Hou Hsiao-hsien.
Actor closely tied to Tsai Ming-liang films from the early 1990s onward.
Loose label for early-1990s filmmakers after the first New Cinema cluster — especially Tsai Ming-liang — working as domestic commercial cinema dried up and festival circuits mattered more.

PRC film generation that emerged in the early 1980s from the Beijing Film Academy after the Cultural Revolution (Chen Kaige, Zhang Yimou, and others). Yellow Earth (1984) is a usual first international marker.
1984 Chen Kaige film, cinematography by Zhang Yimou. A Fifth Generation landmark that traveled festivals in the same decade as Taiwan New Cinema.
PRC Fifth Generation director. Yellow Earth (1984); later Farewell My Concubine (1993).
Hong Kong directors moving from 1970s television into features around 1979 (Ann Hui, Tsui Hark, and others), with a Second Wave into the 1980s-90s.
Hong Kong New Wave director (The Secret, 1979, and later Boat People). Contemporaneous regional peer, not a Taiwan studio product.

American studio period roughly 1967-1980 when conglomerates financed younger directors and antiheroes. By the mid-1980s that bet had tipped toward blockbusters — the Hollywood mode Taiwan New Cinema was not copying.
French late-1950s/early-1960s cluster. The phrase new cinema/new wave traveled; Taiwan 1980s turn had its own studio (CMPC), martial-law context, and literary sources.
Romance novelist whose adaptations were a CMPC and commercial staple before and beside New Cinema.
Ruling party of the Republic of China on Taiwan through the martial-law decades. CMPC sat inside that political economy.
The state governing Taiwan in this lesson’s years. National cinema before the 1980s often meant cinema for that state’s cultural policy and overseas Chinese markets.
Government office that oversaw film policy and guidance in the martial-law and early post-martial-law years. A target of the 1987 manifesto complaint about unclear aims.
Hill town in northern Taiwan. Setting and location for Dust in the Wind and later heavily associated with A City of Sadness tourism.
Capital and New Cinema main urban set: apartments, offices, night streets, and the middle-class lives Yang filmed.

Critical phrase for stories that follow families, workers, and local time instead of leaders’ speeches. Used here for how City of Sadness and related films let political violence arrive through a household.

sections.title: CMPC habits, martial law, and what “national cinema” meant

blocks.text: Before the phrase Taiwan New Cinema stuck, the Republic of China film business had a clear center of gravity. The Central Motion Picture Corporation — CMPC (中影) — was the major state-linked studio. From the 1960s it promoted healthy-realism: films that borrowed the look of everyday life while keeping the social picture clean enough for a martial-law culture industry. Beside that line sat commercial genres audiences already knew how to buy, including Qiong Yao melodramas, comedies, and patriotic pictures. Hong Kong action and comedy imports, and Hollywood bookings, took a large share of the box office. A domestic Mandarin film was often asked to be national in a narrow sense: speak the language of official culture, travel to overseas Chinese markets, and not open subjects the Government Information Office and the censors preferred closed.

Martial law, in force from 1949 until 15 July 1987, is the political frame for that studio habit. It does not mean every film was a propaganda reel. It does mean scripts moved through guidance, and that public history — especially 2/28 in 1947 and the long White Terror — was not ordinary commercial subject matter. National cinema in those decades was less a critics’ aesthetic category than a policy mood: cinema as cultural work for the ROC, produced inside institutions the Kuomintang could see. When audiences drifted toward Hong Kong and Hollywood, the problem for CMPC was industrial as well as ideological. By the late 1970s and early 1980s the studio’s own managers and writers were looking for cheaper, younger, more local films that might bring people back without simply copying a Hong Kong gag reel.

blocks.alt: Stone memorial sculptures of bound figures in an outdoor plaza in Taipei, with high-rises beyond the trees.
blocks.caption: Memorial to the Victims of the White Terror, at the northwest corner of Taipei Jieshou Park area, photographed in 2014. The sculptures and plaza are later public memory, not a 1980s film set. They stand here because martial-law repression is the political weather New Cinema inherited — including the histories early features could not yet name openly.
blocks.credit: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0

blocks.text: That inheritance matters for how to read the “before.” Healthy-realism had already claimed the word realism. New Cinema would claim a different realism: location sound and rooms that were not moral examples, speech in Taiwanese as well as Mandarin where the story needed it, and — later — histories the studio system had kept off the marquee. The break was not a sudden private indie scene. It began, awkwardly, inside CMPC’s own attempt to renew product.

sections.title: 1982 as a door, 1987 as weather, festivals as a path

blocks.text: The conventional opening date is 1982: In Our Time, a CMPC omnibus with four segments by Tao Te-chen, Edward Yang, Ko I-chen, and Chang Yi. The Chinese title means a story that unfolds with time; the English title nods at Hemingway. The industrial fact is simpler. CMPC, under managers such as Ming Ji and with writers including Hsiao Yeh and Wu Nien-jen in the pipeline, backed young directors to shoot everyday lives across decades of postwar Taiwan. The film’s success — limited booking windows and all — showed that a quieter, more observational domestic picture could still move tickets. It also gave critics a cluster they could name.

1983 widened the door. Growing Up, directed by Chen Kun-hou with Hou Hsiao-hsien among the writers, treated coming-of-age as something you could watch without a healthy-realism sermon. The Sandwich Man packaged three Huang Chun-ming adaptations directed by Hou, Tseng Chuang-hsiang, and Wan Jen — nativist literature moved onto film with CMPC still on the letterhead. These are not underground tapes. They are studio-backed turns that changed what a local film was allowed to look like: non-professional or understated acting, location shooting, long takes that let a street or a kitchen run longer than continuity editing would usually permit.

blocks.alt: Hou Hsiao-hsien, Tseng Chuang-hsiang, and Wan Jen seated at a long table with microphones at a festival forum.
blocks.caption: Hou Hsiao-hsien, Tseng Chuang-hsiang, and Wan Jen at an open forum on The Sandwich Man during the International Film Festival of India in Goa, 29 November 2010. The suits and banner are 2010. The three names are the 1983 omnibus fact: early New Cinema as a shared CMPC package, not a lone genius myth.
blocks.credit: Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (India) / Wikimedia Commons / GODL-India

blocks.text: Through the mid-1980s the look hardened into a critical vocabulary. Hou’s Dust in the Wind (1986) followed young people from Jiufen into Taipei work. Yang’s Taipei Story (1985) and The Terrorizers (1986) treated the capital’s apartments, offices, and chance meetings as form, not postcard. Critics talked about the long take as a concrete choice: stay with a corridor, a meal, a mute photographer’s waiting, instead of cutting every glance into Hollywood continuity. History from below is a useful phrase for the same habit when the subject turns political — let a family absorb the news, rather than stage a leader’s speech. None of this required a single switch on 15 July 1987, when martial law ended. The lift mattered as context: more room to speak, more risk that films would test what could be shown. It was weather, not a clapperboard.

The cultural fight that does have a date on paper is the Taiwan Cinema Manifesto of early 1987 — sometimes called the “Another Cinema” manifesto — drafted around a late-1986 gathering associated with Edward Yang and published in January 1987. Roughly fifty filmmakers and cultural workers argued that policy swung unclearly among propaganda, industry, and culture; that mass media preferred star gossip to film as art; and that much local criticism pushed Hong Kong and Hollywood models. They asked for space for another cinema. Many historians read the document less as a birth certificate than as a hinge: the first wave already existed, domestic returns were softening, and the argument was about whether that cinema would be allowed to survive as culture rather than only as a failed commercial genre. Festival paths — especially European competitions — became one practical answer when Taipei bookings thinned.

blocks.alt: Aerial view of 228 Peace Memorial Park in Taipei with the central monument and tree canopy, city towers beyond.
blocks.caption: 228 Peace Memorial Park in Taipei Zhongzheng District, photographed in 2005 from the Shin Kong Life Tower observation deck. The park was New Park under martial law; it was renamed after democratization. The monument at center is later memory architecture. A City of Sadness (1989) put 2/28 on screen before this skyline view became a tourist caption.
blocks.credit: Allen Timothy Chang / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0

sections.title: Many names, and three films to look at closely

blocks.text: The field is wider than two auteurs. Hou Hsiao-hsien and Edward Yang are the names international festivals repeated first. Beside them: Wan Jen and Tseng Chuang-hsiang on The Sandwich Man; Wang Tung in CMPC literary and historical films; Wu Nien-jen in the script department and as Hou’s collaborator; Chu T’ien-wen as Hou’s other constant writer; Chen Kun-hou on Growing Up; Sylvia Chang as actor and producer in Yang’s That Day, on the Beach and across the industry’s star-producer lane. Tsai Ming-liang belongs at the edge of this lesson — early 1990s Second New Wave aftershock, not the 1982 omnibus door. The point of listing is industrial: New Cinema was a cohort overlapping CMPC, literature, and later independent production, not a club with one address.

A City of Sadness (1989) is the film to deepen first. Hou, with Wu Nien-jen and Chu T’ien-wen writing, follows the Lin family across the mid-1940s: Japanese surrender, Nationalist arrival, 2/28, and the first cold years of repression. Tony Leung Chiu-wai plays Wen-ching, a deaf-mute photographer; much of what politics does to the household arrives as letters, absences, and rooms that hold still. The long take here is not decoration. It is how you watch people wait for news they cannot control. Venice gave the film the Golden Lion in September 1989 — the first Taiwanese Golden Lion — which meant the island’s forbidden history traveled as festival prestige at the same moment domestic audiences argued over it. Jiufen locations later became tourism; the film’s fact is older and colder than the souvenir shops.

blocks.alt: Close portrait of Hou Hsiao-hsien in 1989, jacket collar up, facing left of frame.
blocks.caption: Hou Hsiao-hsien in 1989, the year of A City of Sadness and the Venice Golden Lion. A journalist’s outdoor portrait, not a still from the Lin family story.
blocks.credit: Gorup de Besanez / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.text: Yang’s Taipei films are the second deepening. Taipei Story (1985) pairs Tsai Chin with Hou as a former baseball player drifting through property deals and old loyalties while the city rebuilds around them. The Terrorizers (1986) crosses a novelist, a doctor, a photographer, and a young woman whose phone calls puncture other lives; Taipei is mapped as simultaneous rooms rather than a single hero’s route. A Brighter Summer Day (1991) then widens the canvas to early-1960s youth — school uniforms, street gangs, American rock — and a murder case that becomes national allegory without ceasing to be a long, concrete adolescence. Against Hollywood continuity, Yang’s camera often holds a hallway or a night street until social geometry becomes visible. Urban form is the subject: who owns the apartment, who still talks about baseball, who gets left in the frame after the cut that never comes.

blocks.alt: Edward Yang in a tuxedo holding a Golden Horse trophy in 1994.
blocks.caption: Edward Yang with the Best Original Screenplay Golden Horse for A Confucian Confusion, 10 December 1994. The tuxedo and trophy are an awards-night document from after Taipei Story and The Terrorizers. The face is the director who had already made Taipei a formal problem for cinema.
blocks.credit: Wu Chi-chang / Taiwan Cultural Memory Bank / public domain

blocks.text: The third deepening is the CMPC-to-festival path itself. Early New Cinema needed the state studio’s schedules and money. International recognition — Venice for City of Sadness, later Cannes attention for Hou, Criterion and archive restorations decades on — is how the films kept circulating when Taiwan’s commercial screens preferred other product. Dust in the Wind and The Puppetmaster show Hou’s other mode: rural and colonial memory, Li Tian-lu’s testimony, trains and glove-theatre stages, still built from long looking. Sylvia Chang’s presence in Yang’s first feature reminds you that stars and producers shared the same years; Wan Jen’s career reminds you the omnibus was a group door. Theory talk that stays honest stays concrete: a long take is a decision about time; history from below is a decision about whose kitchen the news enters; both are arguments with continuity cinema’s habit of explaining too fast.

blocks.alt: Wan Jen outdoors in a dark jacket, facing the camera, at a film festival in 2010.
blocks.caption: Wan Jen at the Festival international des cinémas d’Asie in Vesoul, France, 2010. A later festival portrait of one of The Sandwich Man’s three 1983 directors.

blocks.alt: Sylvia Chang at a microphone in 2011, dark blazer, short hair.
blocks.caption: Sylvia Chang at the Hong Kong International Film Festival, 2011. Actor-producer in Yang’s That Day, on the Beach (1983) and a durable industry presence across the New Cinema years. The microphone and backdrop are 2011; the career overlap is 1980s fact.

sections.title: Same years: Fifth Generation, Hong Kong waves, Hollywood after New Hollywood

blocks.text: Look out from Taipei, not from a worksheet that assigns one peer per continent. In the People’s Republic, the Fifth Generation was leaving the Beijing Film Academy into features: Chen Kaige’s Yellow Earth (1984), with Zhang Yimou photographing northern landscape and folk form, became an international marker the same decade Hou and Yang were redefining Taiwanese screens. The state, the censorship map, and the market were different. The shared fact is calendar and festival: both cinemas learned that European competitions could carry films their home booking systems undervalued.

blocks.alt: Chen Kaige speaking into a microphone at a film festival panel, glasses and dark jacket.
blocks.caption: Chen Kaige speaking after a screening of Yellow Earth (1984) at the 50th Hong Kong International Film Festival (photograph dated 2026). The panel furniture is contemporary. The film named in the program is the 1984 Fifth Generation landmark — a PRC contemporaneous argument, not a Taiwanese sequel.
blocks.credit: Fred Cherrygarden / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.text: Hong Kong New Wave had already moved from television (especially TVB) into features around 1979 — Ann Hui, Tsui Hark, and others — with a Second Wave carrying into the 1980s. Those films shared a language market and a ferry distance with Taipei; they did not share CMPC’s martial-law brief. For Taiwanese producers the practical pressure was often Hong Kong’s commercial pull on local screens. That is a regional industrial fact, not a claim that Hui equals Hou.

In the United States, New Hollywood was already ending. The director-driven studio bets of the 1970s had tipped, after Jaws and Star Wars, toward wide-release blockbusters; Heaven’s Gate (1980) is the usual tombstone in that American story. By the mid-1980s Hollywood’s loud export mode was the blockbuster and the high-concept booking, not Easy Rider. Taiwan New Cinema did not grow as a franchise of that American decade. It grew as a local answer to CMPC habits, Hong Kong imports, and a political thaw — while French New Wave remained a circulating name for young cinema, useful as analogy and misleading as origin myth. This lesson’s related links are for those honest comparisons: Nouvelle Vague as a traveling label; New Hollywood as the Hollywood mode that had already turned toward blockbusters when Taipei’s new films were finding their feet.

sections.title: Second New Wave, commercial drought, festival auteurs

blocks.text: By the early 1990s the first-wave energy had scattered. Domestic commercial cinema entered a long drought; Hong Kong and Hollywood continued to dominate bookings. Tsai Ming-liang’s early features — Rebels of the Neon God, then Vive L’Amour (1994), which itself took a Golden Lion — are usually filed as Second New Wave: even emptier Taipei rooms, bodies that wait, Lee Kang-sheng as a recurring presence. Hou and Yang became festival auteurs whose films might matter more in Paris or New York than in a Saturday Taipei multiplex. Yang’s Yi Yi (2000) arrived as a late summation. Later Taiwanese festival careers grew from this split: local screens thin, international prestige thick. The New Cinema years remain the hinge when local lives and difficult history got a camera style equal to them.

blocks.alt: Tsai Ming-liang in a dark coat at Tokyo Filmex in 2013, looking toward the camera.
blocks.caption: Tsai Ming-liang at Tokyo Filmex, 2013. A Second New Wave aftershock portrait — years after In Our Time — of the director of Vive L’Amour. The coat and backdrop are 2013; the empty-room cinema is the 1990s fact.

blocks.text: If a film holds a Taipei hallway or a family meal longer than continuity editing would usually allow, what history is it asking you to notice that a faster cut would skip?
